title: Short-Term Plasticity (Dynamic Gain at the Synapse)
excerpt: The preceding subsections have focused on mechanisms that produce lasting changes in cortical synaptic efficacy—voltage/Ca2+-dependent rules, three-factor consolidation, and inhibitory plasticity. But cortical signal transmission is also continuously reshaped
html:
The preceding subsections have focused on mechanisms that produce lasting changes in cortical synaptic efficacy—voltage/Ca2+-dependent rules, three-factor consolidation, and inhibitory plasticity. But cortical signal transmission is also continuously reshaped on much faster timescales by short-term plasticity (STP): the rapid, reversible, use-dependent changes in effective synaptic strength that occur with every spike and recover within tens of milliseconds to seconds, with augmentation and post-tetanic potentiation extending into the seconds-to-minutes regime. The core biophysical mechanisms of STP—facilitation (residual presynaptic Ca2+ enhancing release probability on subsequent spikes), depression (vesicle depletion, release-site refractoriness), augmentation, post-tetanic potentiation, and postsynaptic receptor desensitization—are developed in detail in "The Fundamentals" and are not recapitulated here. The emphasis in this subsection is cortex-specific: which cortical pathways depress, which facilitate, which postsynaptic targets they differentially recruit, how neuromodulatory state retunes these temporal filters, and what this means for the moment-to-moment flow of predictions, prediction errors, recurrent context, and inhibition through cortical circuits.

STP is not a durable memory mechanism; it does not store the cortex’s generative model. Its importance is that it determines the momentary transfer function of every pathway through which cortical computation flows 1, 2. A strongly depressing synapse transmits the first spike in a train faithfully but progressively attenuates subsequent spikes; a facilitating synapse does the opposite, transmitting early spikes weakly but amplifying later ones. In practice, most cortical synapses exhibit a mixture of facilitation and depression, producing a characteristic net transfer function (net facilitating, net depressing, or mixed/biphasic) that depends on initial release probability (p0p_0), vesicle pool size, calcium dynamics, and receptor desensitization kinetics. The effective STP phenotype is therefore not a binary label but a continuous, tunable filter 3. The cortex-specific question is how this filter is distributed across the canonical pathways of cortical computation—feedforward, recurrent, feedback, and inhibitory—and how it dynamically retunes the effective gain of each pathway from one spike to the next 4, 5.

The best-studied sensory-cortex example is thalamocortical and closely related feedforward excitation. When probed from rest, core thalamocortical synapses onto layer-4 cortical neurons (e.g those transmitting retinal data) are typically strong and strongly depressing, and this depression contributes directly to rapid sensory adaptation in vivo 6, 7. However, this should not be stated as a universal fixed law. In mouse barrel cortex, lemniscal thalamocortical synapses are indeed depression-dominated when stimulation begins from rest, but during ongoing stimulation they show a continuum of interval tuning, including facilitation after prior depression; the effective cortical filter therefore depends on recent history, not just synapse class 8. A closely related intracortical feedforward example is the L4→\toL2/3 pathway in V1: it shows robust short-term depression, and recent in vitro/in vivo work argues that this depression is sufficient to explain a substantial part of stimulus-specific visual adaptation and temporal integration in awake cortex 9. The safest cortical summary for this motif is therefore: sensory feedforward pathways often begin in a depressing regime that suppresses sustained or redundant drive and emphasizes changes, onsets, and pattern irregularities—but the realized filter can become richer under ongoing activity, with the effective transfer function shifting as a function of the recent stimulus history rather than remaining fixed by synapse class alone 6, 8, 10.

In contrast to core thalamocortical and many local intracortical excitatory synapses, long-range corticocortical projections are not exclusively depressing and in several cases show robust short-term facilitation during repeated activation. Using selective optical stimulation, Martinetti et al. found strong facilitation in reciprocal vS1↔\leftrightarrowvM1 projections as well as in the sensory-sensory vS1→\tovS2 pathway 11. In mouse auditory cortex, direct A1↔\leftrightarrowA2 corticocortical connections have been shown to comprise two response classes, one of which showed smaller initial EPSPs together with paired-pulse facilitation and metabotropic glutamate receptor recruitment 12. An analogous mixed organization was reported for reciprocal V1↔\leftrightarrowV2 connections in mouse visual cortex, where corticocortical inputs again included a facilitating/Class-2 subtype alongside a depressing/Class-1B subtype 13. Thus, facilitation recurs across multiple interareal corticocortical pathways, although often as one component of a heterogeneous projection rather than as a uniform property of every synapse. Computationally, facilitating corticocortical channels preferentially transmit sustained or repeated evidence, allowing ongoing activity in one cortical area to accumulate influence over another across the course of a train 11, 12, 13.

A related association-cortex motif appears in prefrontal recurrent excitation. In rat and ferret medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), recurrent pyramidal subnetworks include strongly facilitating synapses with pronounced augmentation and post-tetanic potentiation; these subnetworks are distinct from more sensory-like depressing subnetworks and are plausible contributors to sustained activity and working-memory-related temporal integration 2, 14. Computational modeling supports this link: facilitating recurrent excitatory synapses, particularly when combined with augmentation-timescale dynamics, can sustain delay-period activity and support robust working-memory representations without requiring fine-tuned attractor parameters—providing a synaptic substrate for temporal integration that complements classical persistent-activity models 15, 16.

From these two motifs, one potential cortex-specific contrast emerges: sensory and feedforward cortex often uses STP to attenuate repeated input (emphasizing transients and novelty), whereas association and prefrontal subnetworks more often exploit facilitation and augmentation to preserve or amplify long-range and/or temporally extended context 2, 14, 11.

Another one of the most important cortex-specific findings is that STP depends strongly on the postsynaptic target cell. In classic paired recordings from neocortical L2/3, the same class of pyramidal neuron produced facilitating EPSPs onto bitufted/SST-like interneurons but depressing EPSPs onto multipolar/PV-like interneurons 5. Related work in layer-4 neocortex suggests that STP can depend strongly on the identity of the postsynaptic inhibitory target: synapses involving fast-spiking (FS)/PV cells were reported to more often show relatively reliable, depressing transmission, whereas pathways involving low-threshold spiking (LTS)/SST-like cells more often showed weaker initial responses with facilitation 17.

Thalamic recruitment shows the same logic. During behaviorally relevant thalamocortical trains, PV/FS interneurons are activated rapidly but only transiently because their thalamic inputs depress strongly, whereas a subset of SOM/SST interneurons are recruited with a delay through facilitating and summating EPSPs, producing a shift from early perisomatic/feedforward inhibition toward later dendritic inhibition 18. More recent auditory-cortex work formalizes this computational implication: excitatory input to PV neurons generally depresses, whereas excitatory input to SST neurons facilitates, and this differential STP can account for temporal-context effects such as rapid adaptation versus delayed facilitation of cortical responses 19.

STP should therefore be understood not merely as "synapses weaken or strengthen briefly," but as a microcircuit routing rule that determines whether a spike train first recruits fast perisomatic veto (via depressing PV pathways), delayed dendritic gating (via facilitating SST pathways), or recurrent amplification—and how this recruitment sequence evolves over the course of a stimulus 5, 17, 18.

Neuromodulation adds to the picture: in cortex, neuromodulators do not simply multiply synaptic amplitudes; they can change the train dynamics themselves–the effective STP rule. Acetylcholine can modulate synaptic transmission in a pathway- and receptor-dependent manner rather than acting as a uniform gain signal: in mouse visual cortex, cholinergic modulation differed across stimulated pathways and could either facilitate or depress responses depending on ACh concentration and muscarinic receptor subtype, consistent with the idea that cholinergic state dynamically reweights cortical input streams 20. Norepinephrine shows equally pathway-specific effects. In auditory cortex, NE changes inhibitory train dynamics differently for apical versus basal pathways onto L2/3 pyramidal cells: it selectively enhances facilitation in layer-I-evoked inhibitory responses while increasing depression in layer-II/III-evoked inhibitory responses during high-frequency trains 21. Available cortical evidence suggests that dopamine can also interact with short-term synaptic dynamics in a pathway-, receptor-, and cell-type-specific manner. In prefrontal cortex, D1/D5 receptor activation has been reported to slightly reduce initial non-NMDA transmission while enhancing the sustained NMDA component during 20 Hz trains, effectively favoring persistent over isolated excitatory input 22; complementary work found that D1 activation at excitatory inputs onto fast-spiking interneurons selectively reduced the first EPSP in a 20 Hz train while sparing later responses 23; and a further study showed that D2 activation in layer-V PFC pyramidal neurons altered spike-train dynamics in a subtype- and frequency-dependent manner 24. The takeaway is therefore that neuromodulators reparameterize the temporal filters implemented by local cortical synapses, often in a pathway-, compartment-, and cell-type-specific manner, thereby changing which streams dominate over the course of a burst or behavioral state 25, 21, 26. STP and long-term plasticity are not independent layers. STP shapes the actual voltage and Ca2+ trajectories seen during induction trains, so it changes the effective pairing statistics that downstream LTP/LTD mechanisms experience; conversely, presynaptic forms of long-term plasticity can alter the subsequent STP profile of the synapse 10, 27. A useful example is layer-5 neocortex, where long-term changes have been shown to include a presynaptic component identifiable through altered coefficient of variation and altered short-term plasticity dynamics, implying that some "long-term learning" rewrites the synapse’s future short-term filtering properties 27. The correct framing is therefore that STP is part of the induction state for cortical long-term learning, and it is itself one of the variables that long-term plasticity can tune; in that sense, some long-term learning may act by rewriting the synapse’s future short-term temporal filter, not only its baseline efficacy 27, 28.

The cortex-specific STP motifs reviewed above converge on several computational functions that are directly relevant to the optimization architecture developed in the preceding sections:

Rapid adaptation and novelty/transient sensitivity in sensory cortex. Depression at thalamocortical and intracortical feedforward synapses suppresses repeated input while preserving strong responses to abrupt changes and temporally irregular features. This implements an input-specific dynamic gain control that automatically emphasizes the unexpected–functionally equivalent to a local, activity-history-dependent filter that highlights prediction-violating transients at the earliest cortical processing stage 6, 9, 10.

Dynamic E/I reweighting across a spike train. Because PV-linked pathways have been shown to depress and SST-linked pathways have been shown to facilitate, the balance of soma-targeting versus dendrite-targeting inhibition is itself history-dependent. Over the course of a stimulus, cortical integration shifts from an early regime dominated by fast perisomatic/feedforward inhibition (PV-mediated) toward a later regime in which contextual and dendritic gating (SST-mediated) becomes progressively more influential–changing the cortical integration window from early fast veto toward later contextual/dendritic gating 17, 18, 19.

Extended temporal integration in association cortex. Facilitating recurrent and long-range corticocortical synapses allow repeated or sustained activity to become progressively more effective, providing a plausible synaptic substrate for delay-period maintenance and context accumulation in prefrontal and association circuits. Where depressing sensory synapses strip away redundancy and emphasize novelty, facilitating association-cortex synapses do the converse: they accumulate evidence over time, letting sustained or repeated signals build influence—a temporal integration profile well matched to the working-memory and decision-making computations these areas support 2, 14, 15, 11.

In sum, STP is best described as the fastest layer of the cortical adaptive-gain stack: it operates at every synapse, requires no instructive signal, and automatically adjusts the effective weight of each pathway based on its recent activation history. Combined with pathway- and cell-type-specific profiles, STP dynamically reshapes E/I balance, interneuron recruitment order, and the relative weighting of feedforward versus feedback streams on a moment-by-moment basis—complementing the slower neuromodulatory, oscillatory, and structural precision mechanisms covered in the preceding sections.
